title: Saying "a" — the plain form
summary: The earlier blanket noun + mo indefiniteness rule is under review. No automatic indefinite form should be generated from it.
note: Speaker sentence evidence and linguistic descriptions of focus challenge the earlier generalization. Preserve recorded noun forms; do not extend either an indefinite or a focus analysis to every occurrence.

title: Saying "the" — it is part of the noun
summary: There is no Kasem word for "the". Definiteness is marked on the noun itself, and unlike the indefinite mo it changes from noun to noun according to the noun's class. So "the" cannot be translated on its own; what can be recorded is the definite form of each noun, which is what the dictionary now collects.
note: This is why "the" was retired from the guided word queue: the question had no answer and was rank 1 of 15,000, so every new contributor met it first.

title: Noun classes
summary: Kasem nouns fall into classes, and the class decides how the definite and plural forms are built. The inventory below is generated from the classes recorded in kasem-morphology.ts and is deliberately incomplete: it is being built from definite forms contributed by speakers rather than assumed in advance.
note: Kept as a draft until the inventory is worth publishing. Do not hand-edit the nounClasses array on the published document — seed-grammar.mjs generates it from NOUN_CLASSES so the two cannot drift.

title: English prepositions
note: Deliberately empty. English prepositions do not map one-to-one onto Kasem and several are not separate words at all, which is why asking the queue for "the Kasem for of" collected nothing. The triggers are listed so those rows leave the queue; the explanation is left for a Kasem speaker to write rather than guessed at here.

title: Joining words
note: Deliberately empty, on the same terms as the prepositions above.

title: Saying "is" - often there is no verb "to be" at all
summary: English uses "is" for everything. Kasem does not, and for a physical state it does something quite different: the sensation becomes the subject of the clause and the person who feels it becomes the object. "The big boy is hungry" is built as "hunger has the big boy". There is no word standing where the English "is" stands, so "is" cannot be translated on its own - what can be recorded is how each kind of statement is built.

examples.kasem: kana mo jege bakeira kamunu kom
examples.note: word for word: hunger PART has boy big the
word for word: hunger PART has me. `ne` is the object form - `a`/`amo` is "I" as a subject

note: Draft scoped to the contributed hunger examples. Other physical states and other uses of English be require their own evidence.

title: The particle `mo`
summary: Linguistic research describes mo as a focus marker. Applicability to the project dialects and individual constructions requires reviewed contextual evidence.
note: Dropping mo does not by itself establish its function. Focus marking may be required in a context. Do not infer the segmentation of amo or a universal placement rule from spelling alone.

title: The order of a Kasem clause
summary: Subject, then verb, then object, as in English. Inside a noun phrase the order is the other way round from English: the adjective follows its noun, and the definite marker comes last of all. So "the big boy" is `bakeira kamunu kom` - boy, big, the. Knowing the words is not knowing the sentence, which is why the project records whole sentences with a word-for-word line under them.

examples.note: word for word: boy big the

note: Draft, from a single contributed sentence. One noun phrase is enough to show the order and nowhere near enough to know what happens with two adjectives, with a possessor, or in the plural.
